content: Iron(II) sulfate, also known as ferrous sulfate or copperas, is a chemical compound with the formula FeSO4. It is most commonly encountered as a blue-green heptahydrate. In its anhydrous crystalline form, the standard enthalpy of formation is -928.4 kJ/mol, and the standard molar entropy is 107.5 J/(K·mol). Iron(II) sulfate exists in various hydrated forms, which occur naturally as minerals. These include: FeSO4·H2O, known as the mineral szomolnokite. FeSO4·4H2O. FeSO4·5H2O, known as the mineral siderotil. FeSO4·7H2O, known as the mineral melanterite. When heated to 90°C, the heptahydrate form loses water and converts into the monohydrate form, which is colorless and also referred to as green vitriol or copperas. Iron(II) sulfate is produced as a byproduct during the pickling of steel in sulfuric acid baths, a process used to prepare steel for plating or coating. It is also commercially synthesized by oxidizing pyrite or by reacting iron with sulfuric acid. This compound has several important applications: 1. Water Treatment: It is used in water purification processes, particularly for flocculation and the removal of phosphates in municipal and industrial sewage treatment plants. This helps prevent eutrophication in surface water bodies. 2. Reducing Agent: It is employed as a reducing agent, especially for the reduction of chromates in cement. In the field of nutrition, ferrous sulfate is widely used to treat iron-deficiency anemia. Common side effects of this treatment include nausea and epigastric discomfort, which can be mitigated by taking the medication at bedtime. Historically, in the 18th and 19th centuries, ferrous sulfate was administered indiscriminately to enslaved individuals by untrained persons, often causing severe nausea, vomiting, and even death. Today, it is also used to fortify foods with iron, such as enriched cornmeal found in products like Cheetos. In the realm of coloring, ferrous sulfate has been used in the production of inks, particularly iron gall ink, which was widely utilized from the Middle Ages until the American Revolution. It also serves as a mordant in wool dyeing. During the 18th and 19th centuries, it played a role in the china blue process for applying indigo dye to fabrics. This method involved reducing indigo to leuco-indigo using ferrous sulfate baths, followed by reoxidation in air. While this process allowed for sharp designs, it could not achieve the deep hues of other dyeing methods. Additionally, ferrous sulfate is used to stain concrete with a yellowish rust color and to give maple wood a silvery appearance in woodworking. Other uses of ferrous sulfate include: Horticulture: It is applied as a lawn conditioner and moss killer. Photography: In the late 19th century, it was used as a photographic developer for collodion process images. Turbine Maintenance: It is sometimes added to the cooling water in brass turbine condenser tubes, where it forms a protective, erosion-resistant coating on the inner surfaces of the tubes.
